claim: Hepatocytes are regarded as the only effective cell source for cell transplantation to treat liver diseases.
source: Hepatocytes are regarded as the only effective cell source for cell transplantation to treat liver diseases; however, their availability is limited due to a donor shortage.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: The availability of hepatocytes is limited due to a donor shortage.
source: Hepatocytes are regarded as the only effective cell source for cell transplantation to treat liver diseases; however, their availability is limited due to a donor shortage.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the field.

claim: Mature rodent hepatocytes can be reprogrammed into progenitor-like cells with a repopulative capacity using small molecule inhibitors.
source: We recently reported that mature rodent hepatocytes can be reprogrammed into progenitor-like cells with a repopulative capacity using small molecule inhibitors.
evidence: This is a reference to the authors' previous work.

claim: Hepatic progenitor cells can be obtained from human infant hepatocytes using the same strategy as for rodent hepatocytes.
source: Here, we demonstrate that hepatic progenitor cells can be obtained from human infant hepatocytes using the same strategy.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: hCLiPs had a significant repopulative capacity in injured mouse livers following transplantation.
source: These cells, named human chemically induced liver progenitors (hCLiPs), had a significant repopulative capacity in injured mouse livers following transplantation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: hCLiPs redifferentiated into mature hepatocytes in vitro upon treatment with hepatic maturation-inducing factors.
source: hCLiPs redifferentiated into mature hepatocytes in vitro upon treatment with hepatic maturation-inducing factors.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Redifferentiated hCLiPs exhibited cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymatic activities in response to CYP-inducing molecules.
source: These redifferentiated cells exhibited cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymatic activities in response to CYP-inducing molecules and these activities were comparable with those in primary human hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: CYP enzymatic activities in redifferentiated hCLiPs were comparable with those in primary human hepatocytes.
source: These redifferentiated cells exhibited cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymatic activities in response to CYP-inducing molecules and these activities were comparable with those in primary human hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Human hepatocytes are currently regarded as the only competent cell source for transplantation therapy.
source: Human hepatocytes are currently regarded as the only competent cell source for transplantation therapy (Fisher and Strom, 2006); however, their availability is limited due to a shortage of donors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The therapeutic application of hepatocytes is hampered by their inability to proliferate in vitro.
source: Moreover, the therapeutic application of hepatocytes is hampered by their inability to proliferate in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the field.

claim: Primary hepatocytes efficiently repopulate injured mouse livers with repopulation indexes (RIs) > 50%.
source: However, while primary hepatocytes efficiently repopulate injured mouse livers (repopulation indexes (RIs) > 50%), the repopulation efficiency of these laboratory-generated hepatocytes is limited, with reported RIs generally less than 5% (reviewed in Rezvani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Laboratory-generated hepatocytes have limited repopulation efficiency with reported RIs generally less than 5%.
source: However, while primary hepatocytes efficiently repopulate injured mouse livers (repopulation indexes (RIs) > 50%), the repopulation efficiency of these laboratory-generated hepatocytes is limited, with reported RIs generally less than 5% (reviewed in Rezvani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The growth rate and proliferative lifespan of PHHs are limited.
source: However, the growth rate and proliferative lifespan of PHHs are limited.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation.

claim: PHHs can be cultured for several passages, but their growth rate is slow (population doubling time of 20–300 days).
source: For example, Yoshizato's group reported that PHHs can be cultured for several passages, but their growth rate is slow (population doubling time of 20–300 days) (Yamasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: A cocktail of small molecule signaling inhibitors reprograms rodent adult hepatocytes into culturable LPCs, named chemically induced liver progenitors (CLiPs).
source: We recently reported that a cocktail of small molecule signaling inhibitors reprograms rodent adult hepatocytes into culturable LPCs, named chemically induced liver progenitors (CLiPs) (Katsuda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a reference to the authors' previous work.

claim: Rat CLiPs extensively repopulate chronically injured mouse livers without causing any tumorigenic features.
source: Notably, rat CLiPs extensively repopulate chronically injured mouse livers without causing any tumorigenic features.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Culture in YAC-containing SHM (SHM+YAC) induced the proliferation of cells that morphologically resembled epithelial cells from APHHs.
source: In contrast with the basal culture medium (small hepatocyte medium (SHM)), culture in YAC-containing SHM (SHM+YAC) induced the proliferation of cells that morphologically resembled epithelial cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Proliferating cells from APHHs cultured in YAC were small and had a higher nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio than hepatocytes, which is a typical morphological feature of LPCs.
source: These cells were small and had a higher nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio than hepatocytes, which is a typical morphological feature of LPCs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment.

claim: Rat and mouse CLiPs exhibited a compact polygonal cell shape delimited by sharply defined refractile borders with bright nuclei in phase contrast images when colonies became densely packed.
source: When colonies became densely packed, rat and mouse CLiPs exhibited a compact polygonal cell shape delimited by sharply defined refractile borders with bright nuclei in phase contrast images (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figures 1B and C.

claim: The morphology of human cells cultured in YAC did not clearly change after colonies became densely packed, unlike rat and mouse CLiPs.
source: However, unlike rat and mouse CLiPs, the morphology of human cells did not clearly change after colonies became densely packed (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: One of three lots of APHHs formed proliferative and densely packed colonies with hepatocytic morphology upon culture in medium supplemented with YAC and 10% FBS (FYAC).
source: One of three lots of APHHs formed proliferative and densely packed colonies, and exhibited a hepatocytic morphology upon culture in medium supplemented with YAC and 10% FBS (FYAC) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: All three lots of APHHs formed proliferative colonies with hepatic morphologies upon culture in medium supplemented with AC and 10% FBS (FAC).
source: By contrast, all three lots of APHHs formed proliferative colonies with hepatic morphologies upon culture in medium supplemented with AC and 10% FBS (FAC) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The proliferative capacity of hepatic colony-forming cells from APHHs was limited, and the number of these cells markedly decreased after the first passage.
source: However, the proliferative capacity of these hepatic colony-forming cells was limited, and the number of these cells markedly decreased after the first passage, while non-parenchymal cells (NPCs) with non-hepatic morphologies became the dominant population (data not shown).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment.

claim: PHHs derived from young donors are optimal for in vitro expansion.
source: Next, considering the previous finding that PHHs derived from young donors are optimal for in vitro expansion (Walldorf et al., 2004; Yamasaki et al., 2006), we tested whether infant PHHs (IPHHs) expanded more efficiently in the presence of small molecules and FBS.
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with citations.

claim: IPHHs proliferated in the presence of A, YA, AC and YAC as assessed by WST assay.
source: The water-soluble tetrazolium salt-based (WST) assay demonstrated that these cells proliferated in the presence of A, YA, AC and YAC (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: IPHHs proliferated most efficiently in FAC.
source: Consistent with the observations made in APHHs (Figure 1E), these cells proliferated most efficiently in FAC and thus we used this medium in all subsequent experiments.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Robust proliferation of hepatocytes was not supported by culture in the presence of AC or FBS alone, but was synergistically supported by culture in the presence of both AC and FBS.
source: Robust proliferation of hepatocytes was not supported by culture in the presence of AC or FBS alone, but was synergistically supported by culture in the presence of both AC and FBS (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Proliferating cells cultured in FAC spontaneously acquired a hepatocyte-like morphology as colonies became densely packed.
source: Although proliferating cells cultured in FAC did not morphologically resemble hepatocytes when the cell density was low, they spontaneously acquired a hepatocyte-like morphology as colonies became densely packed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: IPHHs proliferated efficiently and became the predominant population over 2 weeks of culture, unlike APHHs.
source: Unlike APHHs, IPHHs proliferated efficiently and became the predominant population over 2 weeks of culture.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment.

claim: FCL, DUX and JFC IPHHs proliferated 49.2 ± 9.34 (at day 14), 46.2 ± 2.12 (at day 14) and 3.66 ± 0.321 (at day 12) folds, respectively.
source: Two other lots of IPHHs (lot DUX from an 8-month-old donor and lot JFC from a 1-year-old donor) (Table 1) also proliferated in this culture condition, although the proliferative capacity varied among the lots: FCL, DUX and JFC proliferated 49.2 ± 9.34 (at day 14), 46.2 ± 2.12 (at day 14) and 3.66 ± 0.321 (at day 12) folds, respectively (mean ± SEM, determined by two repeated experiments for each lot).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment.

claim: FAC enabled two more donors (11 months and 2-year-old)-derived IPHHs and one juvenile donor (7-year-old)-derived hepatocytes to proliferate and spontaneously change their morphologies to hepatocyte-like ones in the densely packed region of the proliferating colonies.
source: We also confirmed by microscopy that FAC enabled two more donors (11 months and 2-year-old)-derived IPHHs and one juvenile donor (7-year-old)-derived hepatocytes to proliferate and spontaneously change their morphologies to hepatocyte-like ones in the densely packed region of the proliferating colonies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Proliferating cells expressed multiple surface markers of LPCs, including EPCAM, CD44, PROM1 (also known as CD133), CD24, and ITGA6.
source: These proliferating cells expressed multiple surface markers of LPCs, including EPCAM, CD44, PROM1 (also known as CD133), CD24, and ITGA6 (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from flow cytometry with reference to Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PHHs before plating minimally expressed LPC markers.
source: It should be noted that PHHs before plating minimally expressed these LPC markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from flow cytometry with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Expression of DPP4/CD26, a general hepatocyte marker, was still preserved in PHHs after a freeze-thaw cycle.
source: Although we used PHHs which underwent a freeze-thaw cycle, we confirmed that expression of DPP4/CD26, a general hepatocyte marker, was still preserved, supporting the validity of this flow cytometry analysis.
evidence: This is a direct observation from flow cytometry.

claim: Expression of many BEC/LPC marker genes was induced during the 2 weeks of culture.
source: Expression of many of these genes was induced during the 2 weeks of culture (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microarray analysis with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: Expression of multiple BEC/LPC marker genes, including EPCAM, SOX9, KRT19, TACSTD2, AXIN2 and PROX1, was increased in cells cultured in FAC.
source: However, expression of multiple BEC/LPC marker genes, including EPCAM, SOX9, KRT19, TACSTD2, AXIN2 and PROX1, was increased in cells cultured in FAC (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microarray analysis with reference to Figure 2E and F.

claim: Expression of EPCAM, SOX9, and KRT19 was affected not only by the presence of AC but also by the culture duration.
source: Of these, expression of EPCAM, SOX9, and KRT19 was affected not only by the presence of AC but also by the culture duration, suggesting that AC-induced expression of these genes during in vitro culture.
evidence: This is an inference from the microarray data.

claim: Expression of AXIN2 and PROX1 was maintained, but not increased, upon culture in the presence of AC.
source: By contrast, expression of AXIN2 and PROX1 was maintained, but not increased, upon culture in the presence of AC.
evidence: This is a direct observation from microarray analysis.

claim: The majority of gene sets enriched in cells cultured in FAC compared to those cultured in FBS were related to hepatic function.
source: Gene signature enrichment analysis (GSEA) comparing cells cultured in the presence of FBS and those cultured in FAC demonstrated that the majority of gene sets enriched in the latter cells were related to hepatic function (Figure 2G, Supplementary file 1), suggesting that AC also helped to maintain the hepatocytic characteristics of cultured hepatocytes.
evidence: This is a direct observation from GSEA with reference to Figure 2G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: AC helped to maintain the hepatocytic characteristics of cultured hepatocytes.
source: Gene signature enrichment analysis (GSEA) comparing cells cultured in the presence of FBS and those cultured in FAC demonstrated that the majority of gene sets enriched in the latter cells were related to hepatic function (Figure 2G, Supplementary file 1), suggesting that AC also helped to maintain the hepatocytic characteristics of cultured hepatocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the GSEA results.

claim: Two small molecules, AC, together with FBS, support the proliferation of hepatic epithelial cells with characteristics of both hepatocytes and LPCs/BECs.
source: In summary, two small molecules, AC, together with FBS, support the proliferation of hepatic epithelial cells with characteristics of both hepatocytes and LPCs/BECs.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings.

claim: IPHHs cultured in FAC for 7 or 14 days formed a cluster distinct from those cultured in FBS based on hierarchical clustering of the whole transcriptome.
source: Hierarchical clustering of the whole transcriptome demonstrated that IPHHs cultured in FAC for 7 or 14 days formed a cluster distinct from those cultured in FBS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microarray analysis with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: APHHs cultured in FAC for 7 or 14 days were not clearly separated from those cultured in FBS based on hierarchical clustering.
source: In contrast, APHHs cultured in FAC for 7 or 14 days were not clearly separated from those cultured in FBS.
evidence: This is a direct observation from microarray analysis.

claim: APHHs are less sensitive to AC than IPHHs.
source: These results suggest that APHHs are less sensitive to AC than IPHHs.
evidence: This is inferred from the hierarchical clustering results.

claim: Pathways enriched for APHHs compared to IPHHs included hepatic function-associated ones.
source: In contrast, pathways enriched for APHHs included hepatic function-associated ones (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from GSEA with reference to Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: APHHs were not susceptible to the pro-proliferative effect of AC.
source: These results suggest that APHHs were not susceptible to the pro-proliferative effect of AC.
evidence: This is inferred from the GSEA results.

claim: Wnt signaling was enriched in IPHHs compared with APHHs (nominal p-value=0.019).
source: GSEA indicated enrichment of Wnt signaling in IPHHs compared with APHHs (nominal p-value=0.019), suggesting that APHHs less efficiently responded to CHIR99021 (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from GSEA with reference to Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 4.

claim: APHHs less efficiently responded to CHIR99021 than IPHHs.
source: GSEA indicated enrichment of Wnt signaling in IPHHs compared with APHHs (nominal p-value=0.019), suggesting that APHHs less efficiently responded to CHIR99021 (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the GSEA results.

claim: TGFβ signaling was enriched in IPHHs compared with APHHs (nominal p-value<0.001).
source: In contrast, to our surprise, TGFβ signaling was enriched in IPHHs compared with APHHs (nominal p-value<0.001) (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from GSEA with reference to Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 4.

claim: Both IPHHs and APHHs upregulated typical Wnt target genes in hepatocytes, such as GLUL and CYP1A2 in the presence of AC.
source: Both IPHHs and APHHs upregulated typical Wnt target genes in hepatocytes, such as GLUL and CYP1A2 in the presence of AC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: LPC-related Wnt-target genes, AXIN2 and LGR5, were expressed at higher levels in IPHHs than APHHs.
source: On the other hand, we found that LPC-related Wnt-target genes, AXIN2 and LGR5, were expressed at higher levels in IPHHs than APHHs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: TGFβ downstream genes were downregulated in both IPHHs and APHHs treated with FAC compared with their FBS counterparts.
source: We also confirmed that TGFβ downstream genes were downregulated in both IPHHs and APHHs treated with FAC compared with their FBS counterparts (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Expression levels of some TGFβ downstream genes, for example VIM, SNAI1 and ZEB1, were higher in IPHHs than APHH.
source: In addition, we confirmed that expression levels of some of these genes, for example VIM, SNAI1 and ZEB1, were higher in IPHHs than APHH, which explains the reason for the enrichment of TGFβ signaling in IPHHs by GSEA (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 4.

claim: mTORC1 signaling was enriched in IPHHs compared to APHHs.
source: Another signaling pathway enriched in IPHHs was mTORC1 signaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from GSEA with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: mTORC1 is activated specifically in pericentral hepatocytes in a Wnt signaling-dependent manner, and suggested to regulate their growth in normal liver.
source: mTORC1 is activated specifically in pericentral hepatocytes in a Wnt signaling-dependent manner, and suggested to regulate their growth in normal liver (Adebayo Michael et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: mTORC1 is essential for BEC expansion during ductular reaction in regenerating liver as well as BEC organoid formation in vitro.
source: mTORC1 is also reported to be essential for BEC expansion during ductular reaction in regenerating liver as well as BEC organoid formation in vitro (Planas-Paz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The low proliferative capacity of APHHs might be partly explained by their lower responsiveness to Wnt signaling.
source: In summary, although a more detailed analysis is needed, the low proliferative capacity of APHHs might be partly explained by their lower responsiveness to Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is a summary statement inferring from the experimental findings.

claim: Proliferative cells spontaneously acquired hepatic morphologies when they reached 100% confluency, even in the absence of hepatic maturation inducers.
source: As noted in Figure 2C, the proliferative cells spontaneously acquired hepatic morphologies when they reached 100% confluency, even in the absence of hepatic maturation inducers (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, middle panels for each lot).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The morphological change to hepatic morphology was more evident in the presence of hepatic maturation inducers.
source: However, this morphological change was more evident in the presence of hepatic maturation inducers (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, right panels for each lot).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells acquired a polygonal and cytoplasm-rich morphology in the presence of hepatic maturation inducers, which is similar to that of PHHs.
source: In particular, cells acquired a polygonal and cytoplasm-rich morphology, which is similar to that of PHHs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Expression of representative hepatic marker genes, including ALB, TDO2 and SERPINA1 was increased after hepatic maturation induction.
source: Accordingly, microarray analysis confirmed that expression of representative hepatic marker genes, including ALB, TDO2 and SERPINA1 was increased after hepatic maturation induction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microarray analysis with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of the BEC/LPC marker genes including SOX9, KRT19, and KRT7 was decreased after hepatic maturation induction.
source: In contrast with the hepatic marker genes, expression of the BEC/LPC marker genes including SOX9, KRT19, and KRT7 was decreased, suggesting that the proliferative cells lost their BEC/LPC phenotype and acquired a mature hepatic phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microarray analysis with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The proliferative cells lost their BEC/LPC phenotype and acquired a mature hepatic phenotype after hepatic maturation induction.
source: In contrast with the hepatic marker genes, expression of the BEC/LPC marker genes including SOX9, KRT19, and KRT7 was decreased, suggesting that the proliferative cells lost their BEC/LPC phenotype and acquired a mature hepatic phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression changes.

claim: The characteristics of Hep-i(+) cells were relatively similar to those of PHHs based on hierarchical cluster analysis.
source: Hierarchical cluster analysis of genes that were differentially expressed between cells cultured in the presence of hepatic maturation inducers (Hep-i(+)) and cells cultured for the same duration in the absence of hepatic maturation inducers (Hep-i(-)) indicated that the characteristics of Hep-i(+) cells were relatively similar to those of PHHs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from hierarchical cluster analysis with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Overrepresented pathways in Hep-i(+) cells in comparison with Hep-i(-) cells were associated with the immune response and metabolic processes.
source: Overrepresented pathways in Hep-i(+) cells in comparison with Hep-i(-) cells were associated with the immune response and metabolic processes (Figure 4E), both of which are important functions of the liver.
evidence: This is a direct observation from pathway analysis with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Overrepresented pathways in Hep-i(-) cells in comparison with Hep-i(+) cells were associated with developmental processes and morphogenesis.
source: By contrast, overrepresented pathways in Hep-i(-) cells in comparison with Hep-i(+) cells were associated with developmental processes and morphogenesis, implying that Hep-i(-) cells were functionally immature compared with Hep-i(+) cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from pathway analysis with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Hep-i(-) cells were functionally immature compared with Hep-i(+) cells.
source: By contrast, overrepresented pathways in Hep-i(-) cells in comparison with Hep-i(+) cells were associated with developmental processes and morphogenesis, implying that Hep-i(-) cells were functionally immature compared with Hep-i(+) cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the pathway analysis results.

claim: Cell cycle-related genes were overrepresented in Hep-i(-) cells compared to Hep-i(+) cells.
source: In addition, cell cycle-related genes were overrepresented in Hep-i(-) cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 5), which is consistent with the general notion that progenitor cells have a greater proliferative capacity than cells with a more mature phenotype.
evidence: This is a direct observation from gene expression analysis with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 5.

claim: Proliferative cells derived from human hepatocytes via culture in FAC lost their immature phenotype and acquired a mature hepatocyte-like phenotype in response to hepatic maturation inducers.
source: Taken together, proliferative cells derived from human hepatocytes via culture in FAC lost their immature phenotype and acquired a mature hepatocyte-like phenotype in response to hepatic maturation inducers.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings.

claim: Expression of several CYP genes was higher in Hep-i(+) cells than in Hep-i(-) cells.
source: A heatmap revealed that expression of several CYP genes was higher in Hep-i(+) cells than in Hep-i(-) cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microarray analysis with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: CYP genes with higher expression in Hep-i(+) cells included CYP2B6, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, which play crucial roles in metabolic functionality of the human liver.
source: These genes included CYP2B6, CYP2D6, CYP2E1, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, which play crucial roles in metabolic functionality of the human liver (Martignoni et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microarray analysis with a citation for the functional importance.

claim: The enzymatic activities of CYP1A2, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP2D6 and CYP3A were comparable in Hep-i(+) cells derived from lots FCL and JFC as in PHHs.
source: This revealed that the enzymatic activities of CYP1A2, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP2D6 and CYP3A were comparable, if not the same, in Hep-i(+) cells derived from lots FCL and JFC as in PHHs, but were lower in Hep-i(+) cells derived from lot DUX (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from LC-MS/MS analysis with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: CYP enzymatic activities were lower in Hep-i(+) cells derived from lot DUX compared to PHHs.
source: This revealed that the enzymatic activities of CYP1A2, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP2D6 and CYP3A were comparable, if not the same, in Hep-i(+) cells derived from lots FCL and JFC as in PHHs, but were lower in Hep-i(+) cells derived from lot DUX (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from LC-MS/MS analysis with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: CYP1A2, CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 genes were markedly upregulated in cells derived from the three lots in response to the corresponding inducer.
source: These CYP genes were markedly upregulated in cells derived from the three lots in response to the corresponding inducer (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from qRT-PCR analysis with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Enzymatic activities of CYP1A2, CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 were increased in both Hep-i(-) and Hep-i(+) cells upon treatment with the corresponding inducer.
source: Although enzymatic activities of these CYPs were increased in both Hep-i(-) and Hep-i(+) cells upon treatment with the corresponding inducer, these increases were relatively larger in the latter cells (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the changes in gene expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from LC-MS/MS analysis with reference to Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Increases in CYP enzymatic activities upon inducer treatment were relatively larger in Hep-i(+) cells than in Hep-i(-) cells.
source: Although enzymatic activities of these CYPs were increased in both Hep-i(-) and Hep-i(+) cells upon treatment with the corresponding inducer, these increases were relatively larger in the latter cells (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the changes in gene expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from LC-MS/MS analysis with reference to Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Protein expression of CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 in hCLiP-derived hepatocytes was increased in response to the corresponding inducer.
source: We also directly quantified CYP protein expression by mass spectrometry. Protein expression of CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 in hCLiP-derived hepatocytes was increased in response to the corresponding inducer (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from mass spectrometry analysis with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: Activities of the phase II enzymes sulfotransferase (SULT) and UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) were comparable in hCLiP-derived hepatocytes and PHHs.
source: In addition, activities of the phase II enzymes sulfotransferase (SULT) and UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) were comparable in hCLiP-derived hepatocytes and PHHs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from LC-MS/MS analysis with reference to Figure 5E.

claim: hCLiPs differentiate into cells that are metabolically mature after induction of hepatic maturation and thus are potentially applicable for drug metabolism studies.
source: These results demonstrate that hCLiPs differentiate into cells that are metabolically mature after induction of hepatic maturation and thus are potentially applicable for drug metabolism studies.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings.

claim: Cells derived from lots FCL and DUX could be serially passaged until at least passage 10 (P10) without growth arrest.
source: Cells derived from lots FCL and DUX could be serially passaged until at least passage 10 (P10) without growth arrest (Figure 6A) or obvious morphological changes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The population doubling times of FCL and DUX hCLiPs were 1.27 ± 0.0066 and 1.43 ± 0.0086 d, respectively.
source: The population doubling times of FCL and DUX hCLiPs were 1.27 ± 0.0066 and 1.43 ± 0.0086 d, respectively (mean ± SEM, determined by three repeated experiments for each lot).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment.

claim: Non-hepatic cells with a fibroblast-like morphology were observed in hCLiP cultures.
source: However, non-hepatic cells with a fibroblast-like morphology were also observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, arrows), and the percentage of these cells varied among repeated experiments for each lot, as assessed by flow cytometric analysis of the epithelial-cell surface marker proteins EPCAM and CD24 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Cultures of cells from lot JFC contained more fibroblast-like cells than cultures of cells from lots FCL and DUX.
source: Cultures of cells from lot JFC contained more fibroblast-like cells than cultures of cells from lots FCL and DUX (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Upon culture of cells from lot JFC, the percentage of fibroblastic cells increased with the passage number and fibroblastic cells overwhelmed hCLiPs by P5.
source: Upon culture of cells from lot JFC, the percentage of fibroblastic cells increased with the passage number and fibroblastic cells overwhelmed hCLiPs by P5, as assessed by microscopic observation (n = 3 repeated experiments) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and flow cytometric analysis of LPC markers (n = 1 experiment) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: When EPCAM+ cells were sorted from primary hCLiPs at the first passage, proliferative epithelial cells were observed for at least the next three passages (total of four passages) with their population doubling time 1.24 d.

evidence: This is a direct observation from the comparative analysis.

claim: A83-01 is essential to IPHH proliferation as assessed in the mini-screen.
source: Since A83-01 is essential to IPHH proliferation as assessed in the mini-screen (Figure 1A), this small molecule might affect IPHHs in a TGFβ-independent manner.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the mini-screen experiment with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: A83-01 might affect IPHHs in a TGFβ-independent manner.
source: Since A83-01 is essential to IPHH proliferation as assessed in the mini-screen (Figure 1A), this small molecule might affect IPHHs in a TGFβ-independent manner.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that A83-01 is essential for proliferation.

claim: Hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) is used in all four recent studies on in vitro PHH expansion.
source: Notably, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), which is not included in our culture condition, is used in all these four studies, suggesting its critical role.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with cited studies.

claim: HGF plays a critical role in in vitro PHH expansion.
source: Notably, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), which is not included in our culture condition, is used in all these four studies, suggesting its critical role.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with cited studies.

claim: Kim et al. (2019) emphasizes the essential role of HGF in the presence of AC for PHH expansion.
source: Indeed, Kim et al. (2019) particularly emphasizes its essential role in the presence of AC.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Zhang et al. (2018) ascribe the proliferative capacity of PHHs particularly to Wnt signaling.
source: On the other hand, Zhang et al. (2018) ascribe the proliferative capacity of PHHs particularly to Wnt signaling (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Zhang et al. reported that Wnt3a plays an essential role in PHH proliferation, while neither CHIR99021 nor Wnt signaling amplifier Rspo1 substituted for the pro-proliferative effect of Wnt3a.
source: Interestingly, these authors reported that Wnt3a plays an essential role, while neither CHIR99021 nor Wnt signaling amplifier Rspo1 substituted for the pro-proliferative effect of Wnt3a.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Zhang et al. proposed that hypoxic culture condition supports the stable proliferation of PHHs by suppressing PHH senescence.
source: Moreover, these authors proposed a unique idea that hypoxic culture condition supports the stable proliferation of PHHs by suppressing PHH senescence.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Fu et al. demonstrated that a sirtuin suppressor nicotinamide decreases proliferation of PHH.
source: In line with this observation, Fu et al. also demonstrated that a sirtuin suppressor nicotinamide decreases proliferation of PHH.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Nicotinamide is known to induce proliferation of rat hepatocytes.
source: This finding highlights the difference between human and rodent PHHs: nicotinamide is known to induce proliferation of rat hepatocytes (Mitaka et al., 1991) and thus is frequently added to hepatocyte culture medium (including ours), but this may not be the case for induction of PHH proliferation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Nicotinamide may not induce proliferation of human PHHs, highlighting the difference between human and rodent PHHs.
source: This finding highlights the difference between human and rodent PHHs: nicotinamide is known to induce proliferation of rat hepatocytes (Mitaka et al., 1991) and thus is frequently added to hepatocyte culture medium (including ours), but this may not be the case for induction of PHH proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of findings.
